lesson_title: Simple and Compound Events: Trees, Tables and the Taxi You Watched
hook_text: Toss a coin twice. 'Three outcomes, so each is a third,' says half the class. The tree diagram says they just lost the mark.
clip_script: Coin game at the fete: two heads wins a sweet. Half the class says three outcomes — two heads, two tails, one of each — so a third each. Wrong, and here's the proof. Draw the tree. First toss: heads or tails. Second toss: branch again. FOUR paths: heads-heads, heads-tails, tails-heads, tails-tails — a quarter each. 'One of each' is secretly TWO paths wearing one name. That hidden twin, tails-heads, is the mark everyone drops. Two heads? One path. One quarter. Now the taxi. No tree tells you if the 07:00 is full — so you watch. Full on 12 of 40 mornings: 12 over 40, that's 0,3. An estimate, and it sharpens the longer you watch. Coins get theory; taxis get tallies. Last trick: hear 'at least one head'? Don't add three branches. Flip it — the only failure is NO heads, one quarter — so 1 minus a quarter: three quarters. One line. Draw the tree, count the world, and chance stops being luck.
visual_style: A coin flipping in slow motion over a fete stall, branching into a glowing tree of four paths with the forgotten tails-heads branch flashing; a taxi tally sheet filling morning by morning; the words AT LEAST ONE flipping over to reveal NONE.
mood: Playful but exacting — the friend who wins the fete games because they counted first.
pacing: Quick setup, a freeze on the wrong 'third each' answer, satisfying slow reveal of the four paths, brisk through the taxi tally to the complement flip.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count your chances before you spend your ticket.
